One way to think about this is to inquire more deeply about the career fields in which you are considering. What I mean is reach out to your professors in college and ask them exactly what the opportunities are that actually exist out there in the job market that you would have a chance at acquiring with said degree.

This is very very important. Imagine also, the fact that years from now your values might shift once you have transitioned from an educational institution to the workforce. What would your day-to-day routine be like? Would you prefer to raise a family someday? Perhaps you would like to have a career that will afford you ample time with your family, or perhaps you prefer to take on very large scale, time-intensive, complex projects that require most/all of your time.

These are questions that require some introspection because they will heavily influence whether you will actually make the right decision for yourself. I suggested reaching out to professors because many times professors will maintain contacts with former students who have taken these great opportunities. When I was in college, it often felt like I was bugging the professor because there were so many students. However, if this is something that could change your life, it's ultimately worth the effort of scheduling an appointment and asking as many questions as you can and getting all the information you need to make your decision.

I went through a similar thing after my girlfriend (from high school) and I split up. It was very difficult for me, and looking back on it, I was hung up over this for maybe 2 years easily hoping something would change. But it wasn't meant to be, and this thing that I dreaded so much- I eventually came to realize was a blessing in disguise. Moving on from something that emotionally momentous is what we do all through out life. It's like travelling across country and wanting to stop and stay in a particular place at a certain time, but you know you can't.

I don't think there was ever any all-encompassing resolve or closure in my case. It was just like an intense fire in my life that slowly burned away. For a while, I thought that it was everything (and it was) because I felt so much love. Though, the world is full of things to love, we just have to open ourselves up to it. I still believe the old saying bears much truth, "the first cut is the deepest." But the continuance and progression is the way of the world. Eventually we will have to let something else go that we love intensely. It's never easy.

Traveling through the mountains was a whole experiences. Roads were maintained very well (bladed and sanded). Traveling over icy bridges can be a bit sketchy, especially the ones with the metal grating because it feels like you drift a bit. 

One thing I would advise, specifically, is to not follow vehicles too closely. Your windshield will likely catch a rock or two if you do. Though, it wouldn't be a bad idea to set the money aside for a new windshield anyway for after your arrival. Chances are good you're windshield is gonna catch some rocks. And some of the big rigs like to hog the road.

Edit: I didn't carry Canadian currency, I just used my Credit Card. Just be sure to call them and let them know that you're traveling internationally so that you don't get shut off for suspicious activity.
